https://www.critic.co.nz/culture/article.text: News Features Culture Columns Contact Advertise News Tips Culture Critic Te Ārohis Step-by-Step Guide to Becoming a LinkedIn Influencer As students enter university, many (hopefully) age out of Snapchat, and are introduced to a new beast: LinkedIn. If you thought sending streaks was as bleak as it gets, the corporate world has blessed us by making its very own social media platform. The thought of scrolling through the achievements of a balding 40-year-old accountant might make you laugh (or cry), but the job market is fucked – and we’re all expected to play along. At some point between first year and graduation, everyone collectively decides it’s time to become “professional”. Commerce students suddenly start talking about networking. That one guy who somehow landed an internship after first year becomes the authority on ‘building your professional persona’. Your lecturers remind you to keep your LinkedIn profile up to date, and before you know it, you’re seriously considering whether changing your profile picture will make you more employable. People in the industry love to tell you that jobs aren't about what you know anymore, but rather about who you know. Unless you’re lucky enough to be born a nepo baby, you gotta make waves in the corporate world somehow. Turns out the best place to do that is a website where everyone pretends accepting an internship is the defining moment of their life. It might all feel deeply embarrassing, but if everyone else is doing it, you may as well lean in. This may not help you snag a grad role the same way as family connections or a 9.0 GPA would, but desperate times call for desperate measures. When life gives you lemons, make LinkedIn posts. Step 1. Polish Up The Profile 💅 If you’ve somehow managed to avoid making a LinkedIn profile until this point: congratulations! Unfortunately, you have around 30 seconds until a prospective Deloitte intern corners you in the Business School foyer and tells you it’s “literally your living CV – super essential”. Your first job is to find a profile picture. This means trawling through your camera roll until you discover the one photo where you’re not clutching a beer bottle, wearing sunglasses indoors, or sporting pupils the size of coins. Then it's time to fill in your experience, which is where LinkedIn really comes into its own. You delivered flyers? Sounds like you were a Logistical Media Distributor . Bagged groceries at Woolies? That’s a customer-facing role involving spatial packaging solutions in the grocery industry. Worked behind a bar? Congratulations, you’ve got experience operating in a fast-paced, stakeholder oriented environment. If you’re feeling extra fancy, chuck in a few skills. Opened Excel a couple years back in a tutorial? That’s database management and quantitative analysis. Sent a couple of emails during your summer job? Professional written communication. Managed to get through a group project without crying or venting to your flatmates? Successful collaborative leadership. Don’t sell yourself short. As a LinkedIn influencer, your goal is to make everyone your age feel insecure at their own lack of achievements, accolades, and vocabulary. You’ve got this! Step 2 - Connect, connect, connect! 🤝 Forget everything Instagram taught you. On LinkedIn, sending requests to complete strangers isn't awkward – it's expected. Invite everyone to connect. Lecturers, graduates, tutors, flatties, people you met once at a careers expo and anyone remotely connected to the industry you think you might end up working in. The more connections you have, the more people will see your posts. The strange thing is that nobody questions it. In any other context, it would be so fucking bizarre to walk up to someone you’ve never spoken to and ask if they’d like to stay professionally connected forever. On LinkedIn, they’ll probably accept within a few hours and never think about it again. Before long, you’ll have hundreds of connections – most of whom you wouldn’t recognise if they sat next to you in St Daves. And, as soon as you get to 500 connections, it just says 500+. 501 connections is the sweet spot #networking. As an added bonus, LinkedIn is excellent for a cheeky social media stalk. Your lecture crush you’ve never spoken to? You can find out exactly where they’ve worked, what they studied, and every skill they’ve ever claimed to have mastered. Curious what your ex has been up to? They’ll happily announce every career milestone in chronological order. Just make sure your profile viewing is set to private first. There’s nothing quite like accidentally appearing in your ex’s mum’s notifications because you got a little too curious. Step 3 - Become A Hypeman 🔥 Once you’ve got more connections than you do actual friends, it’s time to begin making a name for yourself. In the wanky world of business, this is known as “curating a personal brand”. When your mates post, comment the corniest shit you can imagine. There’s something beautiful about the community that is fostered when you congratulate your flatmate’s internship offer mere days after watching them K-hole on a couch. Exclamation marks are essential for every comment. You better lock in and proudly show future employers your lust for life! A singular “congratulations” or “ka pai” isn’t going to cut it: chuck in a few extra words to show how proud you are of them. “It’s been great to see all your hard work pay off” is a solid start – you’ll have comment reactions flooding in at any second. Step 4 - Post Your Smallest Wins 👏 Once you’ve settled into your groove, it’s time to take that scary step and post. A true LinkedIn influencer doesn’t do a once-a-semester recap – post everything. Joining a club exec, winning an award, getting a new job or a promotion are all things that are worthy of a post. A good rule of thumb is that if your mum would dedicate a post to it on Facebook, chances are you should be posting too. Always include a couple photos, as they take up more room on the feed – people will be forced to look at it longer as they scroll past. AI-generated images are tacky, but the same can’t be said for captions. Chug a few litres of water and lean into that ChatGPT style in the name of professionalism – just check out pretty much any other influence for inspiration. Every sentence should end with an emoji. Em-dashes should be standard, and make sure you follow that classic “It’s not x–it’s y!” sentence structure. Step 5 - Become A Thought Leader 🧠 Eventually, you’ll run out of things to announce. This is where those measly casual LinkedIn users are separated from the Big-Dog-Alpha-Thought Leaders. You know which one you want to be. This is where you stop talking about yourself and start posting motivational observations that sound profound without actually saying anything. Leadership isn't about leading. Success isn't a destination. Growth happens outside your comfort zone. Nobody really knows what these posts mean – but that's not the point! They’re vague enough that nobody can disagree with them, but broad enough that people see themselves within your words – kinda like our horoscopes. And let’s be honest: these are the posts collecting hundreds of likes. The funniest part is watching people who spent years mocking their great aunt for posting inspirational Facebook quotes slowly become the exact same people. University has a remarkable ability to convince otherwise normal people that they are more than equipped to be sharing life lessons after three weeks in a graduate programme. Maybe that's just what happens when your entire professional identity revolves around convincing strangers you’re employable. Step 6 - Profit 🤑 If you follow these steps, you’ll soon have hundreds of likes, dozens of congratulatory comments, and, if the stars align, maybe even a graduate interview. Your mates will absolutely take the piss. Screenshots of your “thrilled to announce” post will end up in the group chat, and it’ll definitely be a conversation topic over a bottle of wine. But that's just part of the deal. The strange thing about LinkedIn is that almost everyone agrees it’s cringe, yet everyone does it anyway. Nobody genuinely enjoys writing essays about accepting a summer internship or pretending a two-hour online course changed their perspective on leadership. But because everybody else is perfecting this faux-professionalism, you eventually start doing it too. Somewhere between first year and graduation, you find yourself debating whether “honoured” sounds better than “thrilled”, and wondering if you should post about joining a committee. At the end of the day, LinkedIn is just shitposting in its most neoliberal form. The memes have been replaced with humble-brags, the comment sections filled with forced enthusiasm instead of arguments, and everyone on there is pretending they aren’t just trying to get a job to cover their next rent payment. It might be the least authentic place on the Internet, but if pretending to have a growth mindset gets you employed in this economy, then whatever. Fake it til you make it. Photograph: Cameron Scott/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Glasgow Thousands of Glasgow council workers face pay cuts in one of UK’s biggest fire-and-rehire plans Unison union refuses to ballot members on offer that would make 11% of council employees worse off UK politics live – latest updates Eve Livingston Sun 4 Oct 2026 05.13 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Thousands of Glasgow council workers face being sacked and reappointed under less favourable terms in one of the UK’s biggest ever “fire-and-rehire” exercises, after union negotiations broke down once again this week. About 23,000 workers – all of the council’s non-teaching staff – first heard they were affected last week when talks between the SNP-led council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions fell apart. Those negotiations concerned a new pay and grading system designed to resolve historical pay equality issues. Unison refused to ballot its members on an offer that would mean pay cuts for 11% of council employees, prompting the council to begin issuing fire-and-rehire letters. At the beginning of this week the fire-and-rehire plans were temporarily paused when Unison returned to the negotiating table. But when discussions collapsed again midweek, the council’s leader, Ricky Bell, suggested Unison members could still be fired and rehired while negotiations with GMB and Unite continued. Unison said it was seeking advice on the legality of its members being treated differently based on union membership. An emergency motion by Green councillors to block the scheme was also rejected on Thursday by the council’s city administration committee, with the Glasgow Greens co-leader Anthony Carroll saying the city was “facing a genuine cliff-edge of one of the largest fire-and-rehire schemes in the UK being implemented”. “We are angry and shocked that the SNP administration moved to fire and rehire all 23,000 staff last week despite its own government’s position,” he said, calling on Bell to personally rule out the move. The deputy first minister, Jenny Gilruth, reaffirmed the Scottish government’s view on fire-and-rehire last week, saying “our position is that such a practice does not align with the principles and expected practice of fair work”. On Friday, Gilruth chaired mediation talks between the council and Unison, securing a further pause to fire and rehire for the weekend. But the union said it must be taken off the table permanently for negotiations to be “productive and in good faith”. For those affected, the week’s tumultuous events have caused anger and uncertainty. “It’s been handled terribly,” said one worker affected. “It’s like a rollercoaster ride of anxiety; we can’t plan for anything and nobody knows what’s going to happen next. We are all furious about how we’ve been treated.” One person close to the negotiations said the unions were particularly aggrieved by “the blatant cynicism” of the council’s fire-and-rehire plans, which were communicated to staff in letters sent at the end of September, meaning a required 12-week notice period expires shortly before the practice becomes illegal in January under UK-wide changes to employment law. “We’re talking about a so-called progressive administration who have spent years taking credit for ending the equal pay dispute,” they said. “It beggars belief they would treat workers who are already undervalued and overworked like this.” In 2019, the council agreed to pay more than £500m to 8,000 mostly female workers who had been discriminated against by unequal pay structures. As seen in Birmingham in 2023 , the authority risks financial ruin if it cannot agree a new pay structure after almost a decade of negotiation. “We know equal pay is still an issue local authorities across Britain need to solve,” one union source said. “Council workers everywhere will surely be looking at what’s happening here and feeling very worried about what might happen to them next.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Glasgow city council agreed in earlier negotiations to protect the pay of those facing wage cuts for an extra year, but Unison said they wanted a further year of protection alongside a number of other concessions. Bell said in a statement: “I’m deeply disappointed that, despite the council putting a further year of pay protection on the table, Unison has once again chosen not to put this offer to its members. Taken together with improvements made since August, this represents a package well over £100m in extra pay for our staff.” Bell said some of Unison’s remaining demands were “simply unworkable”. Unison’s Glasgow city branch said: “We want workers who have waited decades for equal pay to receive every penny they are due. But we will not abandon workers facing devastating losses, or the thousands who still don’t know their outcome.” They called for “a properly funded settlement that delivers equal pay without leaving thousands of other workers behind”. Photograph: Dimitrios Symeonidis/Alamy Language Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests Research shows that the best linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds more like non-speech sounds Anna Bawden Tue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google If you want to get really good at French, Arabic or Hungarian, don’t start with rote learning vocabulary and grammar, focus on how they sound instead, research suggests. A new study of how humans learn modern languages has found that the brains of the most talented linguists hear foreign terms as random noise, not words. Normally, when people learn a language, they try to understand it through the sounds of their native tongue. The more different the foreign language’s sounds and pronunciation are from the native language, the harder the new language will probably be to learn. But the best linguists master even the trickiest pronunciation much more easily. ​To find out why, researchers at UCL and Tohoku University, Japan, compared the auditory precision of 67 Japanese learners of English by measuring their ability to detect slight changes in pitch, length and tone, in non-speech sounds. Using functional MRI scans, they measured participants’ brain activity as they tried to distinguish between English vowel sounds that do not occur in Japanese. They found that those with higher auditory precision mastered the pronunciation of new languages faster and more accurately than other learners and relied less on the brain’s left sensorimotor system (involved in language processing) when processing foreign-language sounds. Instead, their brain activity patterns were similar to those that occur when the brain processes non-speech sounds. With less interference from pre-existing patterns of their native language, it was simpler for these learners to accurately process new sounds. In contrast, those with lower auditory precision relied more on the brain’s left sensorimotor network when listening to foreign-language sounds. They used the pronunciation patterns of their native language when processing unfamiliar sounds. The latest findings challenge stereotypes that Britons are less adept at languages. Prof Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, the lead author and professor of second language education at UCL Institute of Education, said: “I do not think British people are biologically bad at languages. The problem is more likely to be that many people receive too little meaningful exposure, combined with teaching methods that do not necessarily train the auditory skills needed to make the most of that limited exposure. “If you only hear and use the language for a small number of hours each week, having a good ear may make a much bigger difference. Learners with high auditory precision can make very effective use of relatively sparse input, whereas others may need much more exposure before unfamiliar sounds begin to become established,” he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Açaí, chipotle and gnocchi – and other words you are probably mispronouncing Read more The findings also suggest schools should focus on sounds much more than just grammar and vocabulary when teaching modern languages, he added. “Foreign language education should move beyond an approach based on ‘more practice’ and towards one that develops learners’ ear for language learning in line with their auditory characteristics,” he said. Responding to the findings, Prof Padraic Monaghan, professor of cognition at Lancaster University, said: “Traditional language learning relies on structured practice, but our brains are naturally attuned to acquire languages through exposure. This study confirms how vital listening is to learning, though learners vary in their sound sensitivity at least in the early stages of hearing new language sounds.” ​ Explore more on these topics Language Linguistics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students
